questions.stem: Which of the following defines the signal estimate?
questions.key: An orderly and logical examination of all factors, known or assumed, that may affect the successful accomplishment of the signal support operations mission
distractors: A series of logical steps that ensures all aspects of signal support operations are systematically addressed
A design for a future or anticipated operation that serves as a framework to adapt rather than a script to follow
The set of capabilities that enables signal to support Army operations
questions.explanation: PAM 6-0102 (paras 0302-0303) defines the signal estimate, also called the C4S estimate, as an orderly and logical examination of all factors, known or assumed, that may affect the signal support mission.
why: This defines the signal planning process, not the estimate.
This describes a plan, not the signal estimate.
This defines C4S, the capabilities behind signal, not the estimate.

questions.stem: It is a memory aid for the signal estimate: Mission, Enemy signal capabilities, Troops available, Area of operations and Logistical requirements.
distractors: METT-TC
PACE
OAKOC
questions.explanation: PAM 6-0102 (para 0303) gives the keyword METAL to help the planner prepare the signal estimate in any situation and location. Some older handouts wrote it as MENTAL.
why: METT-TC lists the mission variables (Mission, Enemy, Terrain and weather, Troops and support, Time, Civil considerations), not the signal estimate factors.
PACE is the primary, alternate, contingency and emergency means plan.
OAKOC is the terrain analysis aid under the Terrain and weather variable.

questions.stem: Which of the following defines an assumption in the signal estimate?
questions.key: Something believed true that cannot yet be verified, and that must be valid (likely true) and necessary (needed to continue)
distractors: Something that can be verified and is used as the basis for the signal mission
A broad potential solution to an identified problem
A test of whether a solution is acceptable at all
questions.explanation: The handout says a fact can be verified, while an assumption is believed true but not yet verifiable; a good assumption is valid and necessary, and is replaced by a fact as information comes in.
why: This describes a fact, which can be verified.
This defines a course of action (COA).
This describes a screening criterion, not an assumption.

questions.stem: The S6 analyzes the unit's mission and the commander's intent, determines the specified and implied signal tasks, and states the signal mission. This describes which step of making the signal estimate?
distractors: Gather data and determine possible solutions
Analyze the solutions
Compare the solutions
questions.explanation: In Step 1, Know the problem, the signal officer analyzes the mission and intent, determines specified and implied signal tasks and states the signal mission (problem-solving step: identify the issue).
why: Step 2 assembles facts and assumptions and determines the signal means that could support each COA.
Step 3 determines the advantages and disadvantages of each solution against the METAL factors.
Step 4 compares solutions against evaluation criteria and ranks them.

questions.stem: A signal officer asks whether a proposed solution can be done with the radios, operators, power and funds available. This describes which screening criterion?
distractors: Suitable
Acceptable
Distinguishable
questions.explanation: Feasible asks whether the solution can be done with the radios, operators, power and funds on hand (PAM 3-0201, para 0321, as applied in the handout).
why: Suitable asks whether the solution solves the signal problem and is legal and ethical.
Acceptable asks whether the costs and risks are worth it.
Distinguishable asks whether the solution is significantly different from the others.

questions.stem: A staff officer asks whether commercial networks, power, NTC frequency rules and coordination with PNP and LGU affect the plan. This question belongs to which METT-TC variable?
distractors: Troops and support available
Terrain and weather
Time available
questions.explanation: The handout's signal questions for Civil considerations (ASCOPE) are commercial networks, power, NTC rules, PNP and LGU, and crowded events.
why: Troops and support asks about friendly equipment and personnel status and support from higher and adjacent units.
Terrain and weather asks about line of sight, dead spaces, foliage, propagation and storms.
Time available asks how long it takes to move, install, test and rehearse.

questions.stem: It is a staff section's continuous assessment of current and future operations to determine whether the current operation is proceeding as intended and whether future operations are supportable.
distractors: Decision matrix
Mission analysis brief
Annex H (Signal)
questions.explanation: PAM 3-00 (para 0609) defines the running estimate; the signal estimate is the S6's running estimate and is kept current as the situation changes.
why: A decision matrix is a tool used to compare COAs against weighted criteria.
The mission analysis brief is where the staff presents mission analysis results, including signal inputs.
Annex H is the C4S annex to the order, which the running estimate becomes the basis of.

questions.stem: Which list contains the six paragraphs of the signal estimate in the running estimate format, in order?
questions.key: Situation and considerations; Mission; Courses of action; Analysis; Comparison; Recommendations and conclusions
distractors: Mission; Situation and courses of action; Analysis of courses of action; Comparison of courses of action; Recommendation
Situation and considerations; Mission; Analysis; Courses of action; Comparison; Recommendations and conclusions
Mission; Situation and considerations; Courses of action; Comparison; Analysis; Recommendations and conclusions
questions.explanation: Applied to C4S, the PAM 3-0201 running estimate format has six paragraphs: situation and considerations, mission, courses of action, analysis, comparison, and recommendations and conclusions.
why: This is the traditional five-paragraph C-E estimate, not the six-paragraph running estimate.
Analysis cannot precede courses of action because COAs must be stated before they are analyzed.
Mission follows situation and considerations, and analysis comes before comparison.

questions.stem: Which list contains the five screening criteria for a signal solution?
distractors: Mission, Enemy, Troops, Area of operations, Logistical
Suitable, Feasible, Acceptable, Accurate, Timely
Accurate, Timely, Usable, Complete, Precise
questions.explanation: Screening criteria test whether a solution is acceptable at all: suitable, feasible, acceptable, distinguishable and complete (PAM 3-0201, para 0321).
why: This is the METAL factor list, which structures analysis rather than screens solutions.
Accurate and Timely are qualities of information, not screening criteria.
These are qualities that information must have, not screening criteria.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT usually an advantage when comparing signal COAs?
questions.key: Committing all personnel and facilities early in the operation
distractors: Economy of personnel and facilities that leaves uncommitted assets for continuous operation
Signal sites that meet tactical needs and reduce exposure to enemy ground, air and EW attack
Redundant, independent means (PACE)
questions.explanation: The handout lists committing all personnel and facilities early as usually a disadvantage, together with high EW vulnerability in critical phases and failure to meet the tactical requirement.
why: Economy of personnel and facilities is an advantage because assets stay uncommitted.
Well-sited signal sites that limit exposure are an advantage.
Redundant, independent means (PACE) are an advantage.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes how a COA is chosen in the S6's decision matrix?
questions.key: The lowest weighted total is preferred, since rank 1 is best
distractors: The highest weighted total is preferred, since rank 1 is worst
The COA with the most criteria ranked 2 is preferred
The total makes the recommendation, so the S6 need not explain trade-offs
questions.explanation: In the handout's matrix, ranks are 1 = best, multiplied by the weight and added, and the lowest total is preferred. The matrix supports the recommendation but does not make it.
why: Rank 1 is the best rank, so a high total is the worse result.
Rank 2 is the worse rank on a criterion, so more 2s does not make a COA preferred.
When totals tie, the S6 compares criterion by criterion and explains the trade-off; the matrix does not make the recommendation.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the two ways a signal estimate may be formed (PAM 6-0102, para 0302)?
questions.key: Separate estimates for each signal support service and C4S capability that are then integrated, or a single estimate that considers all means required
distractors: One estimate for the S3 and one for the S2, each revised only at mission analysis
A written estimate prepared before the mission and a verbal estimate given after it
A fixed estimate that is never changed and a running estimate revised each phase
questions.explanation: PAM 6-0102 para 0302 says the estimate may be separate estimates per service and C4S capability, integrated by the signal officer, or a single estimate covering all means. Either way it is revised as the situation changes.
why: The two forms are not divided by staff section, and the estimate is revised as the situation changes.
The forms are not written and verbal; both are revised as new facts are introduced.
The estimate is never fixed; it is revised as the situation changes.
